title: The seventh day (Genesis 2:1–3)
hookLine: God finishes, then stops, and blesses the stopping itself
last: TZELEM ELOHIM — NO TWO FACES ALIKE.

cards: Friday night in a Jewish home. The candles are lit, the table is set.
Someone stands and lifts a full cup of wine, and before any blessing over it, recites three verses from Genesis, the ones right after the six days of making.
In homes that keep this custom, the week closes with those words every Friday night. They tell of the day God stopped.

teach.b: The heaven and the earth are finished, the story says, and all their host. Then, in the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "And on the seventh day God finished His work which He had made." Wait.
Finished on the seventh? Wasn't the work done on the sixth? The rabbis noticed.
Rashi, quoting an older midrash, offers one answer: after six days the world had everything but one thing.
Rest. Menuchah. So on the seventh day rest was created, and only then was the work complete.
A world without stopping wasn't finished. Then: "And God blessed the seventh day, and hallowed it." Hallowed means made holy.

teach.h: THE FIRST HOLY THING IS A DAY.
teach.b: In Hebrew it's the first time anything in the Torah is called holy, and it isn't a mountain, a temple or a person. It's a day. A stretch of time.
The twentieth-century rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel made that detail the heart of his book The Sabbath. One more thing.
Every other day of creation closes with "there was evening and there was morning."

teach.h: AND GOD BLESSED THE SEVENTH DAY.
teach.b: The seventh doesn't. Some readers take that as a hint that the rest it started is still open. The text doesn't explain.
So the story ends not with a final product but with a pause, and the pause is the part that's blessed. Finished isn't when the last thing is made. It's when you stop.

how: On Friday night, many Jews recite Genesis 2:1–3, beginning with the word vayechulu, at the start of kiddush over wine, closing the week with the story of the seventh day.

games.q: what's inside the day — tap the pairs.

s: the seventh day ends with "evening and morning" like the others
it's the only day where the refrain never comes.
the first thing the Torah calls holy is a day
not a place or a person: "and God blessed the seventh day, and hallowed it."
the world was complete after the sixth day
Rashi says one thing was missing: rest. it came on the seventh.

games.q: the text says God finished the work on the seventh day, not the sixth. you're Rashi. how do you explain it?
o: the world was missing rest, and rest was made on the seventh.
God worked a little on the seventh day.
games.why: rest, menuchah, was the missing piece. a world without stopping wasn't finished yet.

practice: Today the practice is simply to stop: put down whatever is in your hands, and don't plan, tidy your thoughts or try to relax properly.
If a task comes to mind, let it wait outside the door; nothing needs making for this minute to be complete. If you pray, the stopping itself can be the prayer.

wordCard.voice: Menuchah: the rest the seventh day needed to be finished. The day God stopped, blessed the stopping, and called a stretch of time holy.

carryVoice: Your line: finished is holy. The Sabbath you met on day eleven starts right here. Day twenty-five.
